trial_name: ACURASYS — Neuromuscular Blockers in Early ARDS (2010)
citation: Papazian L, Forel JM, Gacouin A, et al. Neuromuscular blockers in early acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2010;363(12):1107-1116.
one_liner: In early severe ARDS, 48-hour cisatracurium reduced barotrauma and increased ventilator-free days, with an adjusted reduction in 90-day mortality (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48-0.98, P=0.04).

pico.population: Adults with early severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150, PEEP ≥5 cmH2O, bilateral infiltrates, no left atrial hypertension) within 48 hours of meeting criteria, receiving lung-protective ventilation.
pico.intervention: Cisatracurium 15 mg IV bolus then 37.5 mg/hour infusion for 48 hours, with deep sedation (Ramsay 6).
pico.comparison: Placebo infusion for 48 hours, with same deep sedation and lung-protective ventilation.

background.existing_knowledge: Early ARDS is characterised by severe hypoxaemia, high ventilatory demand, and prominent patient–ventilator dyssynchrony that can undermine lung-protective ventilation. Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) were commonly used to facilitate ventilation and reduce oxygen consumption, but their net effect on patient-important outcomes was uncertain. A key countervailing concern was ICU-acquired weakness/paresis, historically linked to prolonged paralysis and deep sedation.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a time-limited (48-hour) cisatracurium infusion, compared with placebo, reduces 90-day mortality and improves clinically relevant outcomes without increasing ICU-acquired paresis.
background.hypothesis: In patients with early, severe ARDS receiving protocolised lung-protective ventilation, a 48-hour cisatracurium infusion would reduce 90-day mortality and improve outcomes without increasing ICU-acquired paresis.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, investigator-initiated trial in 20 French ICUs (enrolment March 2006 to March 2008); stratified randomisation (centre, age, and duration of mechanical ventilation) with concealed allocation and identical study-drug preparation. No interim analysis; trial completed as planned.
methods.setting: 20 French ICUs, mechanically ventilated ICU patients with early severe ARDS (enrolled within 48 hours of meeting ARDS criteria).

inclusion: no clinical evidence of left atrial hypertension

methods.intervention: Cisatracurium besylate: 15 mg IV bolus then fixed-dose infusion 37.5 mg/hour for 48 hours (no peripheral nerve stimulator monitoring to preserve blinding). Deep sedation targeted during the infusion period (Ramsay sedation scale 6) with analgesia as required. Rescue bolus cisatracurium permitted (both groups) for unsafe ventilatory mechanics despite protocol measures.
methods.comparison: Placebo infusion for 48 hours, with the same protocolised ventilation and deep sedation targets during the blinded infusion period. Rescue bolus cisatracurium permitted using the same criteria as the intervention group.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients, treating clinicians, and outcome assessors/statisticians); neuromuscular monitoring was intentionally not used to limit unblinding risk.
methods.sample_size_power: 340 patients required to detect a 15% absolute reduction in 90-day mortality (from 50% to 35%) with 80% power at the 5% (two-sided) significance level.
secondary_outcomes: ICU-acquired paresis at ICU discharge (assessed in cooperative patients)
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome assessed to day 90; protocol planned longer-term follow-up to day 180 (including pulmonary function testing and functional/quality-of-life measures), not reported in main publication.

headline_bullets: No increase in ICU-acquired paresis among assessable survivors (64.3% vs 68.5% without paresis, P=0.51)

outcomes_table.note: Primary analysis: Cox model adjusted for baseline PaO2/FiO2, SAPS II, and plateau pressure. Unadjusted comparisons less definitive.
Ventilator-free days scored as 0 after death
Composite of survival and ICU length of stay
Nonpulmonary components: cardiovascular, coagulation, hepatic, renal
Includes pneumothorax and other barotrauma events

outcomes_table.outcome: ICU-acquired paresis at ICU discharge (patients without paresis)
outcomes_table.note: Assessed only in cooperative patients (subset of cohort)

safety: ICU-acquired paresis at ICU discharge (assessed in cooperative patients): 64.3% vs 68.5% without paresis (P=0.51)
No signal for increased ICU-acquired paresis among assessable survivors

domains.notes: Centralised randomisation with concealed allocation and stratification (centre, age, prior duration of mechanical ventilation); low risk of selection bias.

Double-blind, placebo-controlled, identical infusions; clinical inference of assignment possible because paralysis suppresses spontaneous effort, but protocol-mandated deep sedation (Ramsay 6) in both groups mitigated risk. Neuromuscular monitoring intentionally not used to preserve blinding.
340 randomised, 1 withdrew consent before receiving study drug; analysis population 177 vs 162. Follow-up for mortality to day 90 complete (objective endpoint).

Lung-protective ventilation delivered with close between-group similarity in key mechanics (tidal volume ~6.5 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure ~24.5-25 cmH2O). Rescue cisatracurium boluses permitted in both arms; used more frequently in placebo arm early (10% vs 22%, P=0.004). Fixed-dose cisatracurium (37.5 mg/hour) without neuromuscular monitoring limited dose individualisation.

Groups generally comparable (age, SAPS II), but baseline PaO2/FiO2 significantly lower in cisatracurium group (106 ± 36 vs 115 ± 41, P=0.03), favouring placebo. Intervention initiated early (within 48 hours of meeting eligibility).
Use of prone positioning and inhaled nitric oxide for refractory hypoxaemia was similar between groups (detailed frequencies in supplementary appendix).

Mortality and barotrauma are objective outcomes; ICU-acquired paresis assessment required patient cooperation and therefore applied to a subset (112 vs 89 patients), introducing potential ascertainment/selection bias for neuromuscular outcomes.

Primary endpoint relied on an adjusted Cox model (covariates: baseline PaO2/FiO2, SAPS II, plateau pressure); while adjustment can increase precision, clinical interpretation depends on confidence that covariate selection and modelling were pre-specified and not data-driven.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity is moderate: randomisation and blinding were strong and major outcomes were objective, but interpretation hinges on the adjusted primary analysis and neuromuscular safety was assessed in a non-random subset of survivors.

domains.notes: Enrolled patients had severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2<150) in well-resourced ICUs, with protocolised lung-protective ventilation and deep sedation during the infusion period.

Findings are most directly applicable to patients with early, severe ARDS where dyssynchrony and ventilatory mechanics threaten lung-protective targets and where a short, protocolised NMBA course is feasible. Contemporary ARDS care emphasises lighter sedation, higher utilisation of prone positioning, and different ventilator management patterns, which may modify the risk–benefit balance.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is reasonable for early severe ARDS in similar ICU settings, but may be limited in milder ARDS, in units prioritising light sedation, or where co-interventions (e.g., early proning) are routinely deployed.

strengths: Clinically important endpoints (90-day mortality, ventilator-free days, barotrauma)
limitations: Modest sample size with lower-than-anticipated mortality (reduced power for the prespecified effect size)
Reliance on an adjusted primary model for statistical significance
Deep sedation mandated during the intervention window (limits applicability to lighter-sedation paradigms)
Neuromuscular weakness outcomes measured only in cooperative survivors rather than the full randomised cohort

critical_appraisal.summary: ACURASYS demonstrated that a 48-hour cisatracurium infusion in early severe ARDS reduced barotrauma and increased ventilator-free days, with an adjusted reduction in 90-day mortality, but the mortality benefit was model-dependent and neuromuscular safety assessment was incomplete; subsequent evidence suggests benefit is context-dependent.
strengths: Objective primary outcome and clinically relevant secondary outcomes
weaknesses: Reliance on adjusted primary analysis for statistical significance
Deep sedation mandated during intervention limits applicability to lighter-sedation practice
Incomplete ascertainment of ICU-acquired paresis (assessed only in cooperative survivors)
Modest sample size with lower-than-expected event rate

sections.authors_conclusion: A short, early cisatracurium infusion in severe ARDS was associated with fewer barotrauma events and more ventilator-free days, alongside an adjusted reduction in 90-day mortality.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: In early severe ARDS with high risk of injurious patient effort, a time-limited (48-hour) cisatracurium infusion may be considered to reduce barotrauma and improve ventilator-free days, but routine use is not supported by subsequent evidence; individualised decision-making within a lung-protective bundle is recommended.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with early, severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150) in ICUs capable of protocolised lung-protective ventilation and deep sedation, where dyssynchrony threatens ventilatory targets.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Routine paralysis for all ARDS patients; the benefit is not universal and may depend on sedation strategy and ARDS phenotype.
implementation_caveats: Deep sedation is required during the infusion period, which may conflict with lighter-sedation goals
Neuromuscular monitoring was not used in the trial; individualised dosing may be considered
Subsequent trials (ROSE) found no mortality benefit with a lighter-sedation strategy, so sedation depth is a key effect modifier
ICU-acquired weakness risk should be monitored, though the trial did not show increased paresis in assessable survivors

controversies.notes: The headline mortality effect relied on the adjusted Cox model; unadjusted mortality comparisons were less definitive, prompting debate about the appropriate evidentiary weight of model-dependent “primary” results in RCTs.

controversies.topic: Deep sedation as a design feature and potential effect modifier
controversies.notes: Deep sedation was protocolised during the 48-hour blinded infusion, raising questions about whether any observed benefit reflects paralysis itself, the mitigation of injurious spontaneous effort, or the broader sedation–ventilation package.

ICU-acquired paresis was assessed only in cooperative patients, which may under-detect weakness in patients who died early, were delirious, or had prolonged coma; this complicates inference about the true population-level neuromuscular safety signal.

Editorial commentary and NEJM letters focused on interpretation of mortality analyses and generalisability, reinforcing the central methodological debate around adjustment, sedation, and neuromuscular outcomes.

A later, larger trial comparing early continuous cisatracurium plus deep sedation versus a lighter-sedation usual-care strategy found no difference in 90-day mortality, challenging routine early paralysis as a universal standard and highlighting sedation strategy as a plausible effect modifier.

Post-ROSE meta-analytic updates incorporate control-arm sedation depth as an explicit heterogeneity driver, and overall support a more conditional, phenotype- and practice-dependent interpretation of early NMBA use in ARDS.

Earlier professional society guidance conditionally supported short-course NMBA in selected severe ARDS; subsequent evidence has reinforced the need for individualised use within a broader lung-protective bundle, rather than automatic paralysis for all severe ARDS.

context_related_trials.relation: A later, larger RCT comparing early continuous cisatracurium plus deep sedation versus a lighter-sedation usual-care strategy (with intermittent NMBA allowed) found no difference in 90-day mortality, challenging routine early paralysis and highlighting sedation strategy as a potential effect modifier.

unresolved_questions: Does the benefit of early NMBA depend on sedation depth?
What is the true population-level neuromuscular safety signal?
Is the mortality benefit real or an artifact of adjustment?
How does early NMBA interact with prone positioning and other co-interventions?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In early severe ARDS, a 48-hour cisatracurium infusion reduced barotrauma and increased ventilator-free days, with an adjusted mortality benefit, but subsequent evidence suggests benefit is context-dependent and routine use is not supported.
